utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Andrew Cayley, Ann Sutherland, and Denise Gustin for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, General Talic is today absent, like he was yesterday, and due to illness. So let's start our business. I think we promised you yesterday an oral decision on the Stara Gradiska motion, which we are going to hand down now. This is, as I explained, an oral decision on a motion filed by the accused General Talic on September 6th, 2002 in which he asks for three remedies from this Trial Chamber. In the first place he asks the Trial Chamber to remove from the transcript of the sitting of September 5, 2002 all references made to the Stara Gradiska military camp, which is situated inter alia in Croatia. In the second place, he asks this Trial Chamber to issue an injunction against the Prosecution barring it from bringing forward in future any evidence related to the said Stara Gradiska military camp. Lastly, this Trial Chamber is being asked by General Talic to postpone the cross-examination of Witness 7.105 until a decision has been taken on the present motion. The basis of General Talic's motion and requests lies in two decisions handed down by this Chamber, on November 23rd, 2001 and December 7th, 2001 respectively. The first of these two decisions had inter alia rejected a request by the Prosecutor to amend para 40 of the then-current indictment - if I remember well, it was the fourth amended indictment - in the sense as to insert a specific reference to "a military detention facility in Stara Gradiska, Croatia (Stara Gradiska military prison)." The second of these decisions highlighted that the ultimate effect of the previous decision of this Chamber was that every reference in para 40 of the fourth amended indictment to the Stara Gradiska military camp was to be struck out in its entirety from the said para 40 and the Prosecution was accordingly instructed to file a corrected version of the fourth amended indictment reflecting what has just been stated. That is, the orders made by the Trial Chamber effectively in its decision on November 23rd. One question to the interpreters: Am I going too fast or is it okay? The French, am I going too fast?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little bit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A little bit, okay. And the Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little bit also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I will moderate my speed. It's to be noted for the record that no written pleadings relative to the present motion were filed but oral submissions were made and heard during yesterday's sitting. The arguments and submissions of General Talic are essentially and comprehensively described and explained in the motion itself and the accompanying annexes, to which this Chamber is making specific reference to avoid repetition. The oral submissions were more or less a short resume of those arguments and submissions. The Prosecution's main arguments are the following. First, although the two above-mentioned decisions of this Trial Chamber have not and are not being contested, the legal consequence does not entail a total restriction or prohibition on the Prosecution from bringing forward all kinds of evidence related to the Stara Gradiska military camp and the events that occurred therein when these prove to be relevant. Number 2, this particular military camp fell under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps of which General Talic had the command and was therefore responsible. Then the Prosecution submits also, in addition, that it had disclosed to General Talic and his Defence team all the documentation in its possession under Rule 66 which tended precisely to prove this fact in a way that he must have been aware of what was being pleaded or asserted by the Prosecution. Lastly, it is being submitted by the Prosecution that in any event, the Prosecution retains its right under Rule 93 to bring forward evidence of a consistent pattern of conduct which is relevant to serious violations of international humanitarian law under the Statute, if these are in the interest of justice and are admitted by the Chamber on that basis. The Chamber believes that it is important to highlight the substance, the real substance, and the gist of the first of the two decisions of its two decisions referred to earlier, and the substance and the gist can be synthesized as follows. First, there was no question at all that the indictment did not specifically allege or plead that the Stara Gradiska military camp was operated or administered by the 1st Krajina Corps, for which General Talic was responsible. Point 2: The submission of the Prosecution that this notwithstanding, the indictment read as a whole made it abundantly clear, that his command, that is General Talic's command, included the facility in Croatia, was not accepted by this Trial Chamber which based its decision inter alia on three basic considerations. Consideration number 1: There was no allegation in the indictment that any of the killings therein mentioned and specified related or were committed in -- to, or in the Stara Gradiska military camp. Consideration number 2: Nor were any of the allegations of the infliction of serious body harm or mental harm brought in and described in the indictment against the two accused related in any way to that particular military camp. Point 3, consideration number 3 of this Trial Chamber in its November 23rd decision, that it could not be inferred from the indictment that an assertion was being made that the 1st Krajina Corps was the particular entity within the VRS which directed the staffing and operation of all the camps or, in particular, the Stara Gradiska military camp. In that particular decision, therefore, this Trial Chamber concluded that the indictment, as it was then, namely this is the 4th Amended Indictment which the Prosecution was seeking to amend, did not plead the material fact, even by necessary implication, which was essential to establish that General Talic was criminally responsible for the events that occurred in Croatia. This Chamber also notes that one of the arguments brought forward by the Prosecution in the course of the pleadings preceding that particular decision of this Trial Chamber, that is, the November 23rd, was precisely that the evidence disclosed to the accused showed or purported to show that the Stara Gradiska military camp was administered by the 1st Krajina Corps and was thus under the direct command of General Talic and, in addition, that persons detained in the Autonomous Region of Krajina were kept in that prison. This same submission, as explained earlier, was repeated here in this courtroom during yesterday's sitting by the Prosecution. This Trial Chamber is bound, and makes it clear that it is bound, by its two previous decisions and as a result cannot allow a situation to obtain whereby what is thrown out of the door as unacceptable and in no unclear terms is then allowed to re-enter through the window. The Trial Chamber has no doubt at all that the overall legal effect of its two previous decisions is that if the decision of this Trial Chamber was that if there is no indication at all in the indictment directly or by implication of any of the material facts mentioned earlier, then consequently the Prosecution is barred from bringing forward evidence tending to prove facts related to the Stara Gradiska military camp or events that may have occurred in that military camp. This also neutralises as a consequence the Prosecution's contention that in any event it could invoke Rule 93 relative to evidence of consistent pattern of conduct. I repeat that there is no pleading in the indictment itself that there was any wrongdoing in the Stara Gradiska military camp. The main submission of General Talic, therefore, is well founded and will be accepted with the following provisos: This Trial Chamber distinguishes between the material facts which are at the foundation of General Talic's motion and facts which are merely historical and pertinent to the witness in question and which need to be retained in the transcript of his evidence for historical and chronicle purposes. It is necessary, for example, to retain in the transcript that he affirms that prior to his transportation to Manjaca camp he was detained in the Stara Gradiska military camp and for how long. Equally important is his statement, his affirmation that during his stay in Stara Gradiska military camp he received some military -- some medical treatment there as well as some other events which fall within the parameters of what has just been stated by this Trial Chamber and which in its opinion would not be objectionable in terms of its two previous decisions. The Trial Chamber will review in detail the entire transcript of the 5th of September and will in due course indicate which parts are accordingly being expunged. For the time being it is being made clear that any reference to who was in control of that camp, who administered that camp, who were the guards, what ill-treatment the witness and others may have received in that camp, the conditions in that camp, and other related facts will be expunged. Concluding, the Chamber decides as following: The first request of General Talic contained in his motion, namely to remove from the transcript of the sitting of September 5 all references made to Stara Gradiska, which is situated in Croatia, is being decided in accordance with the provisos that I have just hinted at. The second request, namely to issue an injunction against the Prosecution, barring it from bringing forward in the future evidence related to Stara Gradiska, is being accepted in the terms of what has been stated before by me in this oral decision. Lastly, the request to have the cross-examination of Witness 7.105 delayed pending the decision, I think it has been superseded by the events and need not be decided and is not being decided. And that determines the matter which this Chamber was seized, and I think we can proceed with further business. So -- yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If it pleases the Court, Your Honours, I would have to -- I have three things which I would like to inform this Trial Chamber about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have -- I have information to give as well, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- I can do it any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to supersede you, of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have -- we have been in contact with our client yesterday in the afternoon. Our client has informed us of the following, which I think would be of importance to this Trial Chamber: Our client is -- has waived his right of presence for the whole week and for the -- for the witness Muhamed Filipovic and two coming witnesses. He is ready to waive his rights in the future as well. What we are suggesting, if this would be acceptable by this Trial Chamber and the other parties in this courtroom, is that each Thursday when we receive the list of the new witnesses which are going to be coming the week after, that we get the specific instructions on these witnesses from our client and inform accordingly the Trial Chamber during the session on Thursday or latest by Monday morning. If that would be acceptable, I think that would resolve a huge procedural problem which we are now facing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take your points one by one. Can I ask you to stop here for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, if you want to answer now, answer now. If you want time to consult with Ms. Korner, then obviously we will give you time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, I mean, Your Honour, I think this issue is of enormous impact in this trial, and I think it's something that needs discussion. I mean, I don't think it's just as straightforward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- as the general giving a waiver that we can carry on with the trial. So I think it needs some thought, certainly in our office before we can give any response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's what I -- I expected. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I was thinking about this last night. Your Honours might want to consider a more informal meeting like we have once had where we can all discuss these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have that in mind, Mr. Ackerman, not -- but not at this particular point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At some point in time I think that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Because there are bound to be developments which are bound to have an impact on what needs to be discussed on several fronts. You know, I mean, it's -- I don't need to go into detail, because everything is very much in the air for the time being and we need to know exactly what the situation will be when it crystallizes. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The second thing: Our client has instructed us to inform this Trial Chamber that he will not undergo another physical exam. He feels that this -- this pain that he's suffering from this kind of exam and the overall -- his -- the overall health situation of his does not permit him in any way to undergo another physical examination of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That goes on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The third thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Registrar, please ensure that this communication by Mr. Zecevic on behalf of his client is in turn communicated as soon as possible to the two consultants that -- to whom I will be referring in due course. Yes, Mr. Zecevic, point three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The point three: We would like to express our -- on behalf of our client and on behalf of the Defence of General Talic our sincere gratitude for -- for the Office of the Prosecutor, the Trial Chamber, and the Registry for providing the medical experts, as we are informed that they are coming today on such a short notice. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So with regard to this, and without going into specific details because otherwise we go into closed session, just for the record, and based on the activities that went on and events that happened yesterday after we rose and in which I was personally involved, most of the time in consultation with the other two Judges - even when I was not, they were eventually informed - the situation as it arose was as follows: I took immediate steps to ensure that while the Prosecution was trying to procure the name of a consultant, of an expert, the Registry, which is perhaps a more complicated entity inside this Tribunal, would do the same with the utmost speed, and I am happy to announce in open court that they did. The cooperation was not only forthcoming but it was also very timely. It transpired at some point in time during the late afternoon, early evening, that I had indicated, particularly knowing that the Registrar is himself Dutch, and with the little information that I had from family sources, that there could possibly be first-class Dutch experts on the subject matter which we discussed yesterday, and the Registrar took the hint and identified a world-leading expert who happens to be Dutch, plus another expert who happens to be Belgian, both of whom guaranteed their presence here today. I was also -- I gave instructions at that point in time to inform the Prosecution that the Registrar had identified two persons, not just one. I don't know what the situation was inside the quarters of the OTP at the time, but it seems that a decision was taken to abandon the quest for a further expert from Germany or from wherever and to accept the two persons that the Registrar had indicated. This is the information that I received at the time. I stand to be corrected if it is not so, but this is the information I received. At that point in time, I had no hesitation at all in communicating that, pending obviously all discussions that would take place this morning, and the two consultants were authorised to come forward. I also authorised the disclosure to them of the documents that Dr. Valke had made available and which we had kept under seal. The reason for doing that was to economise on time, and it was the only practical thing to do in the circumstances. I was then informed that they would be here in The Hague this morning, different times, that they would be in consultation with Dr. Valke himself, that they would have available documentation which they already have, and that they should be in a position to report to us in a short -- by means of a short document during the course of the day. I inquired to see whether this was possible, and they agreed that this would be possible also because I am informed that it was not possible at all for them to delay their stay in The Hague beyond today. So that is the information that I have and that I have handed -- that I am passing on to you. I also gave instructions to the Registrar to contact, through diplomatic channels, the host country, that's the Netherlands, because you know that there is a rule, should we decide to grant provisional release, we cannot do that unless we have heard the host country. I am not yet informed whether a document has arrived, as is usually the case. I did not interfere at all, neither did any of my colleagues, with any communications that may be required with the authorities of Republika Srpska or of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that is something that, Mr. Zecevic, you would need to attend to, and obviously we will understand that it's not our responsibility to do that. Yes, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If it pleases the Court, if I may just for a few minutes inform the Court about this development about the guarantees. Actually, the guarantee of Republika Srpska has been filed yesterday in the afternoon, as indicated in our motion. We just received it, Your Honours, from the locker. And the guarantees of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, where this military medical academy is situated, is due to come today, probably just right now, about 11.00. I was told that it would be faxed directly from the Prime Minister's office of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the ICTY's fax, official fax. Therefore, I believe that both guarantees will be in place this -- today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Zecevic in particular, Mr. Ackerman too, and the Prosecution of course too, but Mr. Zecevic in particular, you will all understand that what I have just described is, in absolute terms, very unorthodox, it's an unorthodox procedure, in that I have authorised two consultants to come over and start doing something, without having first come here and put their names to you, Mr. Zecevic, for your approval. I don't quite -- or at least for your comments. The options were two: Either do it the way we did it or do it the orthodox way, which would have had -- meant wait until this morning, let them come here, prohibit them from doing anything, listen to them and so on and so forth, then reach a decision and so on and so forth. So the sort of ratification of what has taken place will take place ex post, and I hope that that would be agreeable to both Prosecution and both the Defence teams. Otherwise, we will withdraw from our position and resort to the orthodox procedural approach to this problem. But we did what we did knowing that we were adopting a procedure which was the most practical and timely, given the circumstances of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe I have already stated our gratitude to this Trial Chamber and to all the parties involved in that. Since time is of the essence, as we are all aware, of course we don't have any objection whatsoever to the persons, the medical experts, who are to appear before this Court today, of course not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any reservations on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's your initial comments, and I think I should put this on the record just to set the record straight. We as an office spent most of the afternoon trying to find individuals, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I say this not for the sake of credit but simply for who has had communication with these people. We eventually located two Dutch specialists, because other specialists could not come within the short time period. Can I -- I mean we are in open session. It's all right to talk openly about these matters in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Simply don't go into details of medical details.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, we -- the two individuals that we located were Dr. (redacted), who is a leading (redacted), and Dr. (redacted) (redacted) who is from the Erasmus Medical Centre in Rotterdam. We as an office spoke to these people and sought their agreement to come at short notice and give a second and third opinion. We, as an office, have sent out staff to collect them from their respective hospitals to bring them into the Tribunal. We, as an office, have had communications with the prison doctor to organise the cooperation between the parties in respect of the medical documentation that these two individuals need. There is one further matter which I believe will be best addressed in closed session. I can put the Court on notice of something that one of these physicians has required, which may be something, from what Mr. Zecevic has said, the patient is not willing to undergo, but we can talk about that in closed session. Their respective arrivals will be 11.00 and I think 2.00, but their evidence will be heard this afternoon for both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that change anything, as far as you are concerned, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This does not change anything whatsoever. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you want to go in closed session now, Mr. Cayley, and we'll discuss the final point that -- is there something wrong with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I -- I mean, I -- I think what's already been said previously has probably indicated a great deal of information. I've mentioned a condition. I mean, it can be -- it can be redacted. We've asked for it to be redacted. But I can talk in more detail in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay let's go in closed session for a while, and then I think it's -- some people are born unlucky. Two gentlemen have just walked in to follow the hearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was just wondering if private session isn't enough. We don't have a witness. Why do we have to close all the blinds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Wait. Wait. Wait. Would that be okay with you, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll go into private session and not closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25(redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25(redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will now proceed from where we left this morning. We are in open session at the present moment. Is there anything that either the Prosecution or the Defence would like to state?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, other than to say we should go to straight into closed session, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The same applies with you, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Madam Registrar, please, and Usher we will go into private -- to private or closed?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think it makes a ha'p'worth of difference, but closed, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think closed because we are having the witnesses, I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 6.02 p.m., to be reconvened sine die.
